revisions.title: Understand the Saponification section
revisions.summary: Base oils in Saponification determine the alkali requirement. Check their soap chemistry and the lye setting together.
revisions.body_markdown:
Put the base oils used for the soap reaction in **Saponification**. Here, “base oils” includes butters, waxes and fatty acids with verified soap chemistry.

Check their amounts, the lye type and purity, **Lye reduction / excess**, and the dilution-liquid calculation.

Soap percentages marked **% oils** refer to the total base oils in this section. Moving a material to Formula additions changes its calculation role.

After changing amounts or sections, recheck alkali, dilution liquid, warnings and composition. **Nominal superfat** is recipe shorthand. **Estimated free fat** is a concentration in the whole cured bar or finished diluted liquid soap, so its percentage can differ.

revisions.title: Lye reduction, nominal superfat and estimated free fat
revisions.summary: The lye setting, recipe shorthand and fat concentration in the finished soap answer different questions.
revisions.body_markdown:
### Lye reduction / excess

**Your input: how much alkali to use.** Positive values use less alkali than the base oils in **Saponification** need. Negative values add extra alkali: −3% means 3% more than those oils need.

Here, “base oils” includes any butter, wax or fatty acid in Saponification with verified soap chemistry.

### Nominal superfat

**The familiar recipe shorthand: lye reduction + fatty additions, as % of base oils.**

For example, 1,000 g of base oils (770 g shea butter and 230 g coconut oil), 2% lye reduction and 60 g sunflower oil in Formula additions give **2% + 6% = 8% nominal superfat**.

This shortcut is not an exact equivalent lye reduction. Different SAP values mean that equal weights of fatty materials do not need equal amounts of alkali. A fatty acid used for liquid-soap neutralization belongs to that reaction, not to the finishing additions in this shortcut.

### Estimated free fat

**Estimated unsaponified fatty material as a percentage of the whole finished soap.**

In that example, the model leaves about **80 g** of fatty material: 20 g from the base oils + 60 g sunflower oil. With 11% residual water, the cured soap weighs about **1,346 g**. Using the unrounded cured mass, **free fat ÷ cured soap mass × 100 ≈ 5.95% of cured soap**.

The 8% nominal figure uses recipe percentages; 5.95% uses the whole cured soap, including water and glycerin. They answer different questions.

For liquid soap, free fat uses the final diluted batch mass, after neutralization and additions. It counts all modeled remaining fat: base-paste free fat, explicit fatty additions, unreacted fatty-acid neutralizer and fatty acids released from soap by acid conversion. There is no percentage cutoff that removes fat from this estimate.

If excess KOH remains beyond the process calculation tolerance, the free-fat estimate is withheld: that alkali could still react with finishing fats.

Changing residual water or dilution changes the percentage without changing the amount of fat.

### What counts, and what is assumed?

Oils, butters, waxes and fatty acids count when their soap chemistry is verified. Known fatty components of mixtures count too, including a fatty carrier in a fragrance mixture. Water, glycerin and non-fatty components do not count. Check any named materials omitted for missing chemistry.

For bar soap with zero or positive lye reduction, the model treats fatty finishing additions as unreacted. With negative lye reduction, it shares the modeled reaction proportionally between base oils and all saponifiable finishing additions, including fatty carriers in fragrance blends; it does not consume additions first. Liquid soap models paste neutralization before finishing additions.

These are estimates, not measurements or a prediction of which particular oils survive. In cold process, oil added at trace can still react. SAP data alone does not separately quantify naturally unsaponifiable constituents.

revisions.title: Add fragrance and other finishing materials
revisions.summary: Check whether additions use % oils or % final batch. Fatty additions can affect free fat without changing the lye setting.
revisions.body_markdown:
1. Add the ingredient to the correct part of **Formula additions**.
2. Check whether the amount is a weight, **% oils**, or liquid-soap **% final batch**.
3. Review batch totals, nominal superfat and estimated free fat.
4. Recheck **Composition & labeling**, then save.

A 6% fatty addition to 1,000 g of base oils weighs 60 g. With 2% lye reduction, the recipe shorthand is **8% nominal superfat**. That does not mean 8% of the cured bar is free fat.

Oils, butters, waxes, fatty acids and known fatty components of mixtures count when their soap chemistry is verified. Other additions do not automatically count. Check named omissions.

For bar soap with zero or positive lye reduction, the model counts fatty finishing additions as unreacted. Negative lye reduction shares the modeled reaction proportionally across base oils and all saponifiable finishing additions, including fatty carriers in fragrance blends. Liquid soap models neutralization before finishing additions; its free-fat estimate is withheld while excess KOH remains beyond tolerance.

An additions section describes an ingredient's role, not proof that the reaction has finished. In cold process, an oil added at trace can still react.

revisions.title: Why do soap percentages differ between tables?
revisions.summary: Check what the percentage divides by: base oils, the wet batch or the finished soap.
revisions.body_markdown:
The same ingredient amount gives a different percentage on each basis:

- **% oils:** base oils in Saponification, including butters, waxes and fatty acids with verified soap chemistry.
- **Wet batch:** the complete batch before estimated water loss.
- **Cured soap:** the estimated bar after reaction and water loss, including its selected residual water content.
- **Finished liquid soap:** the final diluted batch after modeled neutralization and additions.

**Estimated free fat** divides the remaining unsaponified fatty material by the whole cured bar or final diluted batch. Water, glycerin, soap salts and other retained ingredients contribute to that finished mass.

**Nominal superfat** is recipe shorthand. In the worked example under Lye reduction, 2% lye reduction + a 6% sunflower addition gives **8% nominal superfat**, while about 80 g of free fat in a cured batch of about 1,346 g gives **5.95% of cured soap** at 11% residual water.

Changing only the water content or dilution changes the free-fat percentage without creating or removing fat. Saved formulas retain their own residual-water assumption; a new family default applies to new formulas.

Allergens are already included in their source ingredients. Their declaration rows do not add mass. Ingredients as added describe the inputs; resulting composition includes the reaction assumptions.

Fatty acids inferred from acid conversion appear together as **Estimated free fatty acids**, marked **Composition estimate only**. Their full modeled mass contributes to the composition and the estimated free-fat value. Adding dilution water changes their percentage, not their weight.

That description is not an INCI name and is excluded from the generated ingredient list. Specifically identified added fatty acids and their modeled soap salts keep their own names. When acid conversion exceeds the calculator's existing rounding tolerance, review the neutralizer dose and ingredient declaration. This alert does not set a labeling exemption.

Tiny positive composition values below the table precision appear as **<0.001%**, rather than zero.
